facts.statement: Borogovia lived during the Late Cretaceous Period in what is now Mongolia.
facts.quote: Borogovia is a troodontid theropod dinosaur genus which lived during the Late Cretaceous Period, in what is now Mongolia.

facts.statement: Borogovia lived approximately 70 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous in Asia.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 70 millones de años, en el Maastrichtiense, en lo que es hoy Asia.

facts.statement: Borogovia was about two meters long and weighed approximately twenty kilograms.
facts.quote: Borogovia is about two meters (6 feet) long, weighing some twenty kilograms (forty-five pounds).

facts.statement: The holotype specimen consists of two lower legs, including tibiotarsi, metatarsi, and toes, found in the Nemegt Formation.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, ZPAL MgD-I/174, was found in the Nemegt Formation, dating from the early Maastrichtian. It consists of two lower legs of a single individual, including fragments of both tibiotarsi, the undersides of both metatarsi, and the second, third, and fourth toes of each foot.

facts.statement: The tibiotarsi of Borogovia have an estimated length of twenty-eight centimetres.
facts.quote: The tibiotarsi have an estimated length of twenty-eight centimetres.

facts.statement: Borogovia features a very elongated tibiotarsus, a narrow third toe, and a short, relatively flat claw on the second toe.
facts.quote: The tibiotarsus is very elongated. The third toe is narrow. The second phalanx of the second toe is short. The claw of the second toe is short and relatively flat.

facts.statement: Osmólska suggested that the second toe regained a weight-bearing function to compensate for the weakness of the third toe.
facts.quote: Osmólska claimed that the second toe could not be hyperextended and suggested that it had regained a weight-bearing function, compensating for the weakness of the third toe.

facts.statement: Osmólska assigned Borogovia to the family Troodontidae in 1987, noting it might be a junior synonym of Saurornithoides.
facts.quote: Osmólska (1987) assigned Borogovia to the Troodontidae in 1987, noting that it may be a junior synonym of Saurornithoides.

facts.statement: A 2021 study recovered Borogovia as a member of the subfamily Troodontinae, closely related to Saurornithoides.
facts.quote: In the 2021 description of Tamarro, Sellés et al. recovered Borogovia as a member of the Troodontinae, closely related to Saurornithoides.

facts.statement: A 2021 revision by Cau and Madzia recovered Borogovia as a sister taxon to the subfamily Troodontinae.
facts.quote: Later in 2021, Cau and Madzia revised material of Borogovia and recovered it as a sister taxon to Troodontinae.

facts.statement: Borogovia is classified within the family Troodontidae.
Borogovia is classified within the subfamily Troodontinae.
Researchers have suggested that Borogovia, Saurornithoides, and Tochisaurus found at the same site might be the same species.
facts.quote: Fue encontrado en el desierto de Gobi, en la Formación de Nemegt, en Mongolia, en el mismo sitio se han encontrados el Saurornithoides y el Tochisaurus por lo que es de pensar que los tres sean la misma especie.
